name: snowflake
desc: Pluggable Transport using WebRTC, inspired by Flashproxy
why: Pluggable transport routing Tor traffic through volunteer WebRTC browsers, a fascinating censorship-circumvention protocol door.

brief.what_it_is: Snowflake is a pluggable transport for Tor, written in Go, that lets Tor traffic travel through volunteer-run WebRTC proxies. A blocked user's Tor client finds an available volunteer proxy through a broker, which is reached over a domain-fronted signalling channel. The client and the proxy then open a WebRTC peer connection, and the proxy relays the Tor traffic on to a Tor relay. The repository contains four programs: snowflake-broker, snowflake-client, snowflake-proxy and snowflake-server. The volunteer side can be a browser extension or a standalone proxy.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames Snowflake as combining the advantages of flashproxy and meek: the convenience of meek, but able to support far more users at negligible CDN cost, and the unlimited volunteer proxies of flashproxy without manual port forwarding.
brief.how_it_works: Volunteers visit websites that host the snowflake proxy, as in flashproxy. Tor clients locate available browser proxies through the Broker, which is a domain-fronted signalling channel, and then establish a WebRTC peer connection with the proxy. The proxy connects to a relay and Tor traffic flows over that DataChannel. Domain fronting is only used for brief signalling and NAT piercing, not for carrying the traffic itself.

commands_seen.context: From the Android AAR reproducible build section: creates and provisions the Vagrant VM that can be used as a development environment for the gomobile-based Android build.
From the same section: logs into the Vagrant VM to use it as a development environment.

brief.install_notes: The README does not give client installation steps. For Tor use, you add Bridge and ClientTransportPlugin lines to your torrc, and the README points to a client README for building and running the client, which I did not fetch. Running a proxy can be done in a browser or as a standalone Go program, with setup documented on the Tor community site. Android builds use gomobile to produce shared libraries per architecture. These run in GitLab CI, or in a Vagrant VM. A Docker-based test environment called snowbox is also linked.
brief.standout: Volunteers can run a proxy just by leaving a browser tab open, and Snowflake disguises Tor traffic as a WebRTC video or voice call. Because domain fronting only handles signalling, it avoids the CDN cost that made meek hard to scale.
brief.status: unknown. The official GitLab repository returned HTTP 403, so I could not check its commit or release history. The GitHub mirror README I read (keroserene/snowflake) still has a Travis CI badge pointing to travis-ci.org, which suggests it is old. The snowflake.torproject.org site says Snowflake is 'continuously being improved' and shows a live counter of 127,599 snowflakes, so the deployed project appears active, but I could not confirm dates.
brief.caveats: The brew homepage (torproject.org) is the general Tor Project site, not a Snowflake page, so the Snowflake-specific information came from the README and the snowflake.torproject.org site. The README I read is from a GitHub mirror, and its Travis badge is for a CI service that has since shut down. The README's link for the v2.1 pluggable transports specification has an empty URL, and the torrc manual link points to a 2019 archive. The browser addon cannot be used to circumvent censorship; it is for helping others do so. The Android AAR build needs gomobile and either GitLab CI or Vagrant. The client and proxy setup guides were not read.
quotes: Pluggable Transport using WebRTC, inspired by Flashproxy.
Snowflake combines the advantages of flashproxy and meek.
NATs are no longer a usability barrier - no need for manual port forwarding!
